previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, bilateral lower extremity amputations, chronic systolic heart failure, and chronic kidney disease was admitted for hyperkalemia and acute on chronic kidney failure, following a recent hospitalization for sepsis and acute kidney injury. Her potassium was elevated to 6.8 with a creatinine of 7.5, likely due to incomplete recovery from prior acute tubular necrosis. She was treated with intravenous calcium, insulin, and dextrose in the emergency department, followed by oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate and furosemide during admission. The renal team evaluated her for dialysis but deferred it given her stability and refusal; instead, she was discharged on potassium-lowering medications, including sodium polystyrene sulfonate and sevelamer, with strict dietary restrictions and close outpatient follow-up. Her home medications were adjusted, including discontinuation of gabapentin and continuation of carvedilol and insulin. She was educated on low-potassium and low-phosphate diet, medication adherence, and the importance of nephrology follow-up and lab monitoring. A venous mapping study was completed to assess future dialysis access. She was discharged home with services in stable condition.

PROCEDURE: LEFT INTERNAL JUGULAR TUNNELED HEMODIALYSIS CATHETER PLACEMENT:
___.

INDICATION:  ___ year-old woman with end-stage renal disease.

OPERATORS:  Dr. ___ (fellow) and ___ (attending
physician).  Dr. ___ was present throughout the procedure.

CONTRAST:  None.

MEDICATION:  2 mg midazolam intravenously over 45 minutes, during which the
patient's hemodynamic status was continuously monitored by a trained radiology
nurse.

TECHNIQUE/FINDINGS:

Consent was obtained from the patient after explaining the benefits, risks,
and alternatives.  The patient was positioned supine on the imaging table in
the interventional suite.  Timeout was performed as per ___ protocol.

Under aseptic conditions, sonographic guidance, and after infiltrating the
skin and subcutaneous tissues with adequate amounts of 1% lidocaine, a
micropuncture needle was placed in the patent left internal jugular vein, just
above the level of clavicle.  Sonographic images were obtained prior to and
following needle placement.  A 0.018 inch wire was advanced through the needle
and into the SVC.  After making an incision at the access site, the needle was
exchanged for a 4 ___ micropuncture sheath.  The inner cannula and wire
were removed to place a 0.035 inch ___ wire, which was advanced into the
IVC.  After appropriate measurements, a site was chosen on the left anterior
chest wall.  After infiltrating the skin and subcutaneous tissues with 1%
lidocaine, an incision was made.  The subcutaneous tissues along with proposed
tunnel were infiltrated with a mixture of lidocaine and epinephrine.  A 15.5
___, 23 cm (tip-to-cuff) hemodialysis catheter was tunneled from the skin
incision to exit at the initial puncture site with the aid of a blunt metallic
tunneler.  The micro puncture sheath was then removed to sequentially dilate
the tract under fluoroscopy with 12 and 14 ___ dilators.  A 16 ___
peel-away sheath was then placed.  The inner cannula and wire were removed to
place the tunneled catheter.  The sheath was peeled away.  The catheter tip
was confirmed under fluoroscopy to be in the upper to mid right atrium.  The
catheter was secured with 0 silk stitches.  Ports were aspirated and flushed. 
A single ___ Vicryl subcuticular stitch was placed at the venotomy site. 
Sites were dressed in a sterile fashion.  The patient tolerated the procedure
well.  No immediate post-procedure complications were seen.

Incidental note of left internal jugular central venous catheter with its tip
in the lower SVC is made.

IMPRESSION:

Uncomplicated ultrasound and fluoroscopy-guided placement of a 15.5 ___, 23
cm (tip-to-cuff) tunneled hemodialysis catheter via the patent left internal
jugular vein, and with its tip in the upper right atrium.  The catheter is
ready for use.
